meta.titre: Christian Missionaries in West Africa: aims, problems and achievements beyond the church
meta.sous_theme: Missionary societies, their obstacles and the religious and social results

sections.contenu_markdown: From Freetown to Calabar, schools, churches and hospitals founded by missionaries in the nineteenth century are still part of the landscape, and many West African leaders were educated in mission schools. Examiners ask why missionaries came, what problems they met and what they achieved. A frequent essay asks whether their success was mainly religious, so you must be able to separate religious results from educational, social, economic and political ones.

items: Britain abolished its own slave trade in 1807, and many Christian campaigners wanted Africa to be reached by Christianity and lawful trade instead.
Sierra Leone was founded as a home for freed slaves, with Freetown as its capital.
Missionary societies were organisations, mostly Protestant in the early nineteenth century, that raised funds and sent missionaries abroad.

sections.titre: Christian missions in West Africa: aims, problems and results
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Societies and aims
The **Church Missionary Society (CMS)**, an Anglican society founded in 1799, began work in Sierra Leone in 1804. Wesleyan Methodists worked in Sierra Leone and the Gold Coast, where Thomas Birch Freeman was active from 1838, and the Basel Mission from Switzerland reached the Gold Coast in 1828. Scottish Presbyterian missionaries began work at Calabar in the 1840s. Their aims were to convert people, to help end the slave trade and to spread education and lawful trade. This mixture was often summed up as Christianity, Commerce and Civilisation.

### Problems faced
| Problem | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Disease | Malaria and other tropical illnesses killed many early European missionaries, and West Africa became known as the white man's grave. |
| Hostility | Some rulers and priests of traditional religions saw the mission as a threat to their authority and customs. |
| Language | Missionaries had to learn local languages before they could teach and translate. |
| Customs | Teaching against practices such as the killing of twins, human sacrifice and polygamy brought conflict. |
| Money and distance | Societies depended on gifts from home, and funds and staff were sometimes short. |
| Rivalry | Different churches competed in the same areas. |

### Religious achievements
Churches and congregations grew, and the Bible and hymns were translated into African languages. Africans were trained as teachers and clergy. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Yoruba freed from a slave ship and educated in Sierra Leone, became the first African Anglican bishop in 1864.

### Other achievements
- **Education**: mission schools taught reading, writing and trades. In 1827 the CMS founded Fourah Bay College in Sierra Leone to train teachers and clergy.
- **Social and medical**: missionaries cared for freed slaves, set up dispensaries and campaigned against practices such as the killing of twins, as Mary Slessor did in the Calabar region later in the century.
- **Economic**: printing presses, craft training and support for lawful trade after the end of the slave trade.
- **Political**: schools produced an educated group which later led nationalism. Critics add that missionaries sometimes prepared the way for colonial rule.

### Judging success
Religious success was real but uneven, and in many areas the lasting impact of the missions was in schools, medicine and new ideas. A good answer gives religious and non-religious results and then judges which were greater.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked about the difficulties of early missionaries.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Group problems as natural (disease, climate), human (hostile rulers, customs, rivalry) and practical (language, funds). Give one example in each paragraph and rank the most serious.

variantes.nom: Question beginning Do you agree or To what extent
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a statement says that missionary success was mainly religious, or mainly social.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Take a position in the first paragraph. Give religious results, then educational, social, economic and political ones, and use named examples such as Fourah Bay College or Crowther. Conclude with a ranked judgement, admitting the weaknesses of your view.

sections.enonce_markdown: Assess the view that the main achievement of Christian missionaries in West Africa was in education.

etapes.justification: Assess the view needs a position about education against other achievements.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Position: education was the most lasting achievement, though not the only one.

etapes.justification: Evidence must be named and dated.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Mission schools taught reading, writing and trades, and in 1827 the CMS founded Fourah Bay College to train teachers and clergy. Education also produced a group of educated Africans.

etapes.justification: Comparing achievements is what the question demands.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Religious: new churches, translated Bibles and African clergy such as Bishop Crowther. Social: care for freed slaves, dispensaries and opposition to the killing of twins. Economic: craft training and support for lawful trade.

etapes.justification: A balanced answer admits the weaknesses of the view.
etapes.resultat_markdown: In some regions few people attended schools, and in Muslim areas missions made little progress, so the results were uneven.
Education had the widest and longest effect because it created teachers, clergy and later leaders, but it was linked to religious aims and cannot be separated from them.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer (key points)**: Education was probably the most lasting achievement of the missionaries. Mission schools taught literacy and skills, and Fourah Bay College trained teachers and clergy from 1827. Other achievements were religious (churches, translations and African clergy such as Crowther), social (care for freed slaves and opposition to the killing of twins) and economic (craft training and support for lawful trade). Religious success was uneven and education was tied to the aim of conversion, but the educated group it produced shaped West African society long after the missions.

items.erreur_markdown: Answering a statement about success only with numbers of converts.
items.pourquoi_faux: The question about successes covers social, educational, economic and political results too.
items.correction_markdown: Include several kinds of result and compare them.

items.erreur_markdown: Calling the Church Missionary Society a Roman Catholic mission.
items.pourquoi_faux: The CMS was an Anglican society. Most early missionary societies in West Africa were Protestant.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying Samuel Ajayi Crowther was a European missionary.
items.pourquoi_faux: He was a Yoruba man, freed from a slave ship and educated in Sierra Leone, who became an Anglican bishop.
items.correction_markdown: Present him as an African who shows the growth of African leadership in the church.

items.erreur_markdown: Presenting missionaries as only heroes or only as agents of colonial rule.
items.pourquoi_faux: They brought education and medicine and also, at times, helped to prepare colonial control.
items.correction_markdown: Show both sides and give a judgement.

items.erreur_markdown: Listing disease as the only problem of the missionaries.
items.pourquoi_faux: Hostility, language, customs, lack of funds and rivalry also mattered.
items.correction_markdown: Give several problems and explain each.

items.enonce_markdown: State three problems faced by early Christian missionaries in West Africa.
items.solution_markdown: Award a mark for each of three: **disease such as malaria**; hostility of some rulers or priests; difficulty of local languages; conflict over customs such as the killing of twins; shortage of funds; rivalry between churches.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain how mission education prepared some West Africans for new roles in the nineteenth century.
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for developed points: (1) schools taught reading, writing and trades, so pupils could become teachers, clerks and craftsmen; (2) colleges such as Fourah Bay trained clergy and teachers who served in West African churches and schools; (3) the use of English or of written African languages opened access to wider ideas. **Each role must be linked to a feature of mission education.**

items.enonce_markdown: Assess the view that missionary work did more to change West African society than to win converts.
items.solution_markdown: Plan: converts (growth of churches, translated Bibles, African clergy but uneven success, Islam and traditional religions still strong); social change (schools, medicine, ending practices such as the killing of twins, freed slave communities); economic and political change (lawful trade, an educated elite, a possible link to colonial rule). Judgement: the social and educational changes were wider than the numbers converted, but the two were linked. **Conclusion: missionaries changed society more widely than they changed belief.**

items_markdown: The CMS began work in Sierra Leone in 1804, and other societies including Methodists, the Basel Mission and Scottish Presbyterians followed in the nineteenth century.
Missionaries aimed at conversion, the end of the slave trade and the spread of education and lawful trade.
Main problems were disease, hostility, language, conflict over customs, shortage of funds and rivalry.
Religious results included churches, translated Bibles and African clergy such as Bishop Crowther.
Education, medicine and social change were often the longest-lasting results, so a question on success needs both religious and non-religious evidence.
